analysis.one_liner: Requires the EPA to set an enforceable legal limit on algae toxin in drinking water.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on October 19, 2018, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the EPA to set a health goal and an enforceable national drinking water limit for microcystin, a toxin produced by blue-green algae that can contaminate public water supplies drawn from lakes like Erie. Under the Safe Drinking Water Act, a "national primary drinking water regulation" is a legal limit water systems must meet, unlike the non-binding health advisories EPA has issued for this toxin. The bill was introduced in the last weeks of the 115th Congress, sent to committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People who get their drinking water from lakes and reservoirs prone to blue-green algae blooms, particularly communities on Lake Erie, would gain an enforceable federal limit on microcystin in their tap water instead of the advisory-only guidance that exists today. Water utilities would also gain a clear federal standard to design testing and treatment around.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People drinking from algae-prone water supplies

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to publish a maximum contaminant level goal and issue a national primary drinking water regulation for microcystin toxin, turning current non-enforceable guidance into a legal limit that public water systems must meet.

The deadline is triggered by EPA's first final regulatory determination after enactment, forcing action on a toxin the agency has studied but never regulated, so residents of algae-affected communities would no longer depend on voluntary advisories for safe tap water.

analysis.who_pays: Public water systems would bear the cost of monitoring and, where needed, treating water to meet the new limit, and those costs would largely be passed on to households through water bills. EPA would bear the cost of developing the regulation, and the bill provides no federal funding to help water systems comply.

drawbacks.text: The bill mandates a new enforceable drinking water standard without providing any federal money to help water systems comply; testing and treatment costs would fall on utilities and ultimately show up in customers' water bills.

A federal limit targets the toxin after it reaches drinking water intakes but does nothing about nutrient runoff from farms and lawns that feeds the algae blooms in the first place, so it treats the symptom while the underlying pollution continues.

Small water systems often face disproportionately high costs per customer to meet new standards, and the bill contains no small-system flexibility or compliance timeline beyond the regulatory determination trigger.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit of an enforceable limit on a toxin that has forced entire cities off their tap water is substantial, and drinking water standards are one of the most direct forms of health protection government provides. The honest cost is real but modest by national standards: monitoring and treatment upgrades paid through water bills, with the burden falling hardest on small systems because the bill offers no funding or flexibility. The bill is also narrow, addressing the toxin in finished drinking water but not the runoff that causes the blooms.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final weeks of the session, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marcy Kaptur introduced the bill on October 19, 2018, with five Democratic colleagues as original cosponsors, roughly two and a half months before the 115th Congress expired.
The bill's only action after introduction was referral to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day; the committee took no further action on it.
No hearing was held, no vote was taken in either chamber, and the bill expired on January 3, 2019, when the 115th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Water systems are better off because they never faced a new unfunded federal testing and treatment mandate. Residents of algae-affected communities are worse off, since tap water remains governed by non-binding advisories rather than an enforceable limit on the toxin.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Water systems that avoid a new unfunded mandate

for.name: Rep. Marcy Kaptur
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: Reps. Tim Ryan of Ohio, Debbie Dingell of Michigan, Suzanne Bonamici of Oregon, Mike Quigley of Illinois, and Marcia Fudge of Ohio
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction; the bill ultimately had 6 cosponsors, all Democrats.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on October 19, 2018 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Greg Walden
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no opposition was recorded; all six sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill died quietly in a Republican-chaired committee without anyone going on record for or against it.

industries.note: The bill would have required utilities drawing from algae-prone waters to test for microcystin and treat water to meet a federal limit, costs that would flow to customers through water bills. Utilities also gained clarity, since a federal standard would replace a patchwork of state rules and non-binding advisories.

industries.industry: Agricultural runoff sources (farms and fertilizer users)
industries.note: The bill targets the toxin only after it reaches drinking water systems and does not regulate the nutrient runoff that feeds algae blooms, so the agricultural pollution driving the problem would have faced no new requirements.
